articles.title: Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes appear to launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. The breakthrough could explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will happen.
articles.content:
Astronomers have uncovered a surprising rule that appears to determine when black holes unleash powerful jets of material into space. Even though black holes can differ in mass by millions of times, researchers found that they seem to follow the same fundamental pattern when producing these enormous cosmic outflows.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, suggests that black holes can activate their jets at the same critical stage of their feeding cycle, whether they weigh roughly 10 times as much as the Sun or millions of times more.

The research was led by Dr. Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University's International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) and a Forrest Research Foundation Fellow, alongside co-author Dr. Andrew Mummery of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

The breakthrough emerged from years of studying unusual events in which supermassive black holes tear stars apart. By combining observations from telescopes in Australia, the United States, India, South Africa, and space, the scientists pieced together a clearer picture of how black holes behave as they consume matter.

Surprisingly, the crucial insight did not come while examining a telescope. It happened in a bar in Madrid, where Goodwin and Mummery were attending a scientific conference. During a conversation, they recognized that the same rule known to govern jet formation in relatively small black holes also seemed to apply to their supermassive counterparts.

Why Some Black Holes Erupt Years After Devouring Stars

One of the biggest mysteries the researchers wanted to explain was why black holes do not always launch jets at the same time.

When a supermassive black hole tears apart a star, it sometimes produces a powerful jet almost immediately. In other cases, the black hole appears relatively quiet for months or even years before suddenly producing a detectable radio outflow.

"We were looking at these events and asking why the timing was so different," said Dr. Goodwin.

"Then the pattern became clear. The delayed jets were appearing when the black hole's feeding rate dropped to the same critical point already known from much smaller black holes.

"That was the moment we realized this was not just a quirk of one type of black hole, but it looked like a rule that applied across the Universe."

Although black holes are often portrayed as cosmic vacuum cleaners that swallow anything nearby, their feeding behavior is far more complicated.

As material spirals toward a black hole, not all of it necessarily disappears beyond the event horizon, the boundary past which nothing can escape. Some matter can instead be expelled into space through powerful jets and other outflows.

"When a black hole tears apart a star, it does not swallow everything neatly," Dr. Goodwin said.

"Some of the material is consumed, and some is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows.

"You can think of it as a black hole burp, except these burps can blast material across enormous distances and influence the galaxies around them."

These enormous outflows can carry energy and matter far from the black hole, potentially affecting the surrounding galaxy.

How Scientists Studied Supermassive Black Holes in Action

Astronomers have long suspected that black holes operate according to the same underlying physical laws regardless of their mass. Demonstrating that connection, however, has been difficult.

One major obstacle is time. The feeding behavior of a supermassive black hole can change over thousands of years, making it nearly impossible for astronomers to watch an entire cycle unfold.

Goodwin and her colleagues tackled this problem by examining rare events known as tidal disruption events.

These occur when a star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and experiences such extreme gravitational forces that it is torn apart. Some of the resulting debris falls toward the black hole, temporarily increasing its feeding activity.

Unlike the much longer changes normally associated with supermassive black holes, these dramatic episodes can play out over just a few years. That gives scientists an unusual opportunity to track how a giant black hole responds as its supply of material changes.

The team initially examined 20 tidal disruption events using observations collected in visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and radio wavelengths. They then selected 10 events for which the available data allowed them to reliably estimate both the rate at which the black hole was consuming matter and the timing of its radio outflows.

By comparing these events, the researchers identified a remarkably consistent pattern.

A Universal 2% Rule for Black Hole Jets

The observations revealed two distinct stages during which black holes can produce jets.

The first occurs early in the feeding process, when the black hole is consuming matter at an exceptionally high rate.

The second can happen much later, hundreds or even thousands of days after the star is initially destroyed.

During this delayed phase, jets appear when the black hole's feeding rate falls to approximately 2% of its Eddington limit.

The Eddington limit is a theoretical benchmark describing the point at which the outward pressure produced by radiation balances the inward pull of gravity. Astronomers use it to measure how intensely a black hole is feeding relative to a characteristic physical limit.

What makes the finding especially significant is that the same 2% threshold has already been linked to jet formation in much smaller black holes within our own Milky Way galaxy.

In other words, black holes separated by enormous differences in mass appear to activate delayed jets at essentially the same relative feeding rate.

"These black holes are separated by enormous differences in mass, but they appear to switch on their jets at the same point in the feeding process," Dr. Goodwin said.

"That tells us something fundamental about black holes: the physics does not seem to care how big they are."

The finding provides a potential explanation for an otherwise puzzling observation. Some black holes generate radio jets soon after destroying a star, while others appear inactive before producing powerful outflows much later.

Rather than behaving unpredictably, these delayed eruptions may be governed by a common physical threshold.

Predicting When Black Holes Will Launch Jets

Beyond revealing something fundamental about black hole physics, the discovery could help astronomers make much better use of powerful radio telescopes.

Observing time on major scientific facilities is limited and highly competitive. Researchers must carefully decide which objects to study, how frequently to observe them, and when they are most likely to reveal something important.

If astronomers can estimate when a black hole's feeding rate will approach the critical threshold, they may be able to predict when a delayed jet is likely to appear.

"Radio telescopes are incredibly powerful, but knowing when to look is just as important as knowing where to look," said Dr. Goodwin. "If we can anticipate when a black hole is more likely to launch a jet, we can run better targeted campaigns, waste fewer observations and improve our chances of catching these rare events at the moment they matter most."

This could reduce unnecessary follow-up observations while increasing the chances of detecting rare jet-launching episodes at crucial moments.

The implications are particularly important for Western Australia, which will host the low-frequency component of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), one of the largest and most ambitious radio astronomy projects ever undertaken.

The Australian Government has invested $387 million in the SKA, while the project's total cost exceeds $2 billion. Making more efficient use of such an expensive facility could provide substantial benefits to astronomers and the wider scientific community, potentially allowing more important discoveries to be made with the available observing time.

As the next generation of astronomical surveys identifies growing numbers of tidal disruption events, researchers will face an increasingly difficult challenge in deciding which ones deserve closer attention.

The newly identified relationship between feeding rates and jet formation could provide a valuable guide, helping scientists focus their observations on the black holes most likely to produce detectable outflows.

A Black Hole Breakthrough Driven by Curiosity

Professor James Arvanitakis, Director of the Forrest Research Foundation, said the discovery highlights the importance of supporting early-career scientists who pursue ambitious questions without knowing in advance where the answers will lead.

This kind of open-ended investigation, often described as 'blue sky' research, can produce unexpected discoveries with benefits extending far beyond the original scientific question.

"The Forrest Research Foundation did not fund a predetermined answer, we backed an exceptional researcher with a difficult question," Professor Arvanitakis said.

"That question has led to a discovery of international significance. This is exactly why fundamental research matters - it expands what we know, sharpens how we use major scientific infrastructure and builds capability that reaches well beyond astronomy.

"The fact this discovery was driven from Western Australia speaks to the strength of our research ecosystem, and the value of giving outstanding people a reason to build their careers here."

By linking the behavior of relatively small black holes to that of supermassive giants, the findings strengthen the idea that the same basic physical processes operate across vastly different scales.

They also offer astronomers a more reliable way to anticipate one of the universe's most dramatic phenomena: the moment a black hole begins launching a powerful jet into space.

This discovery has broad implications for astrophysics, improving prediction of cosmic events and optimizing use of major astronomical facilities, thus benefiting the scientific community and expanding fundamental knowledge about the universe.

articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent une règle universelle derrière les éruptions des jets des trous noirs
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les trous noirs sont des objets mystérieux dans l’espace qui envoient parfois de puissants jets de matière. Ces jets peuvent se produire juste après qu’un trou noir ait avalé une étoile, ou des années plus tard. Jusqu’à présent, les scientifiques ne comprenaient pas pourquoi le moment de ces éruptions variait autant.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe d’astronomes dirigée par le Dr Adelle Goodwin a étudié des événements rares appelés événements de perturbation par marée, où une étoile est déchirée par un trou noir supermassif. En analysant des données provenant de télescopes du monde entier, ils ont découvert que les trous noirs de toutes tailles suivent la même règle pour lancer des jets. Plus précisément, les jets apparaissent lorsque le taux d’alimentation du trou noir tombe à environ 2 % d’une limite appelée limite d’Eddington.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle montre que les trous noirs, quelle que soit leur taille, se comportent de la même manière à un moment clé de leur cycle d’alimentation. Elle explique pourquoi certains trous noirs émettent des jets immédiatement tandis que d’autres attendent. Connaître cette règle aide les scientifiques à prédire quand ces jets apparaîtront, facilitant la planification des observations et l’utilisation plus efficace des télescopes coûteux.

**Prochaine étape** – Les astronomes utiliseront cette nouvelle règle pour mieux programmer leurs observations des trous noirs, notamment avec de grands projets comme l’Observatoire du réseau de kilomètres carrés (SKA) en Australie. Au fur et à mesure que plus d’événements de perturbation par marée seront découverts, les chercheurs pourront se concentrer sur ceux qui sont les plus susceptibles de produire des jets, augmentant ainsi les chances de capturer ces rares explosions cosmiques.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques ont découvert une règle commune qui explique quand les trous noirs de toutes tailles lancent des jets puissants, aidant à prévoir ces événements cosmiques spectaculaires et à mieux utiliser les télescopes.

articles.title: IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03308-4Building the Nobel-prizewinning neutrino experiment was a big risk. To continue its success, scientists — and funders — need to stay bold.
articles.content:
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica.Credit: Christopher Michel (CC BY-SA 4.0)

I vividly remember the first time I read one of Francis Halzen’s papers about high-energy neutrinos. It was the late 1990s, and I was an undergraduate student at the University of California, Berkeley. The field of astroparticle physics was young, and Halzen was making predictions that couldn’t be tested using conventional particle accelerators.

On 6 October, Halzen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. The experiment uses sensors embedded in the ice to detect high-energy neutrinos (a type of fundamental particle) that have been blasted towards Earth from distant cosmic accelerators.

Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos

Astroparticle physicists have lots of ideas for experiments that have the same discovery potential as IceCube. For example, the underwater Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) — a collaboration between North America and Europe — is currently under construction off the coast of Vancouver Island, Canada. There are also several projects searching for dark matter (a substance that does not interact with or emit light), including the XLZD Collaboration (a European–North American consortium) and PandaX in China.

However, realizing these experiments is not easy. The story of Halzen and IceCube is a lesson not just about fundamental science, but also about what it will take to build the infrastructure that will support discoveries over the next few decades.

When I first read Halzen’s paper (F. Halzen et al. Astrophys. J. 527, L93–L96; 1999), IceCube was not yet built, but its predecessor, called the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array (AMANDA), was running. The construction of AMANDA cost around US$7 million. This is much less than the $271 million it cost to build IceCube. Nevertheless, realizing experiments at this smaller scale can be difficult. They require more resources than an initial proof-of-concept project, but they are not large enough to make a discovery.

Astronomy’s ‘adrenaline junkies’: Nobel prize captures the thrill of neutrino physics

Many countries face difficult decisions about research funding, and I am concerned that small and mid-scale projects could be an easy target for cuts. For example, the 2023 US particle physics strategic plan (P5) recommended creating a portfolio of small-scale experiments. However, because of budgetary constraints, it is unclear whether the proposed portfolio will go ahead.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the awarding of a Nobel Prize for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a major breakthrough in astroparticle physics with broad scientific significance. It highlights the real-world impact of detecting cosmic neutrinos, which advances fundamental understanding of the universe. The story also emphasizes the importance of continued investment in similar large-scale scientific infrastructure projects, which have the potential to yield transformative discoveries benefiting humanity's knowledge of space and physics.

articles.title: I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen
articles.summary: As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride. Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to […]
articles.content:
As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride. Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon. Over her 20-year career at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, she supported missions across the Space Shuttle Program, the International Space Station, and now she is applying that experience to Artemis.

April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast. The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon. As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowd’s voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet. For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible. For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget.

That moment also offered a pause for reflection on the work that led her there. As the spacecraft offline operations manager, Mjoen coordinates the work that happens long before launch day. By supporting the ground systems’ senior vehicle operations manager, Matt Czech, she develops integration plans and oversees ground operations for Artemis vehicle processing, focusing on booster and Orion spacecraft operations.

Allison Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon. NASA/Amber Jean Notvest

Mjoen began her career as a flight crew systems engineer with United Space Alliance supporting the Space Shuttle Program. Her team handled mission-specific cabin configurations, including the food, spacesuits, cargo, and payloads astronauts needed aboard the shuttle.

After the Space Shuttle Program retired, she supported the International Space Station Program as a payload integration engineer. In this role, she connected experiment investigators with the organizations developing their hardware. She later worked in the Project Office on the Test and Operations Support Contract before joining NASA’s Operations Project Engineering Office, where she served as the Spacecraft Payloads Integration and Evolution Element lead for Artemis I.

“Early on, I thought every decision had to be perfect, but everything is an opportunity to learn, especially the tasks that seem unrelated at the time. It’s about staying curious, working hard, building relationships, and trusting that each step is preparing you for the next one. Allison Mjoen Operations Manager, NASA's Exploration Ground Systems

That preparation took on new meaning when she first supported integrated firing room operations as a certified operations project engineer during Artemis I. Earning the certification was a milestone. Applying it during real time operations brought a new level of responsibility.

“Every decision and communication directly supported the integrated team’s ability to execute safely and properly implement the test procedure,” said Mjoen.

Working at the integration console underscored the importance of preparation, collaboration and trust — lessons she carries into her work coordinating across teams today.

“I get to collaborate everyday with incredibly talented and dedicated people who are all working toward the same goal. It’s especially rewarding to know that our collective efforts directly contribute to the success of the mission.” Allison Mjoen Operations Manager, NASA's Exploration Ground Systems

For Mjoen, the shared experience is part of what makes Artemis so important. As the Artemis program continues, she looks forward to another moment families will be able to share as astronauts return to the lunar surface.

“That single moment captured the imagination of people around the world and showed what is possible when we come together for a bold goal,” she said of the first Apollo Moon landing. “Artemis is creating that kind of moment for a whole new generation, and this time to stay.”

The story contains sufficient context about her career and contributions, emphasizing the meaningful impact of Artemis on future generations.

articles.title: Japan is launching a mission to Mars’s largest moon Phobos
articles.summary: The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century
articles.content:
The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century

Artist’s representation of the MMX Spacecraft JAXA

We may be on the verge of solving the mystery of the Martian moons. On 20 October, the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launches towards the larger of the two moons, Phobos, with the goal of bringing back a sample that may finally explain how Phobos and its sibling, Deimos, formed.

MMX will launch from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan. If all goes to plan, it should arrive at Mars in August 2027, entering an orbit that keeps it alongside Phobos so it can build a detailed map of the surface. Along the way, it will also observe the surface of Deimos.

Once the map is complete enough, the spacecraft’s operators at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will use it to pick out a spot on Phobos for MMX to land. During one or two brief landings, it will take on two tasks: to drop off a small rover called IDEFIX and to pick up samples. The rover is the first anyone has ever placed on such a small cosmic body, so part of its purpose aside from scientific observations is to confirm that a wheeled rover even works on an object with such low gravity.

Advertisement

The samples, though, are the most important part of the mission. MMX has two different sampling devices: one that shoots a puff of gas onto the surface, blowing dust and pebbles back up into a sampling container, and another that blasts a hollow cylinder into the ground to take a sample a several centimetres deep. After the samples are taken, they will be stowed away inside the spacecraft, which will then head back towards Earth. It is expected to arrive home in 2031.

Once these samples get back to Earth and are analysed by scientists on the ground, they should finally solve the mystery of how Phobos and Deimos formed. For more than a century, researchers have debated whether the two are captured asteroids or formed from an impact on Mars, similar to how Earth’s moon formed. On first look, their shapes and surfaces resemble asteroids, but their circular orbits around Mars’s equator are more consistent with the impact hypothesis. Figuring out what they are made of should settle it once and for all.

Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter

This will also help illuminate what the solar system was like billions of years ago when these strange moons formed. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds,” said Tom Statler, part of the NASA team that is collaborating on the MMX mission, in a statement.

If we are very lucky, the samples from Phobos may even contain bonus bits of dust and debris from Mars itself. Impacts on the planet could have launched material into space, which would have collected on the moon’s surface and been preserved there for billions of years. That means that these samples could illuminate not just the history of Phobos and Deimos, but also of Mars.

This has the potential to advance understanding of planetary formation and the early solar system, benefiting the scientific community and humanity's knowledge of space.

It will orbit close to Phobos, map its surface, and then land briefly to drop off a small rover named IDEFIX and collect samples. The spacecraft will return these samples to Earth by 2031.

Scientists will study their composition to see if they match asteroids or material from Mars itself.
